title: We Build Fences Because Children Run
author: Richard Wheadon
summary: This article argues that boundary-testing and rule-challenging behavior in adolescents is not a disciplinary failure but a developmental necessity — the natural expression of the autonomy drive that research identifies as a core psychological need during adolescence. Richard Wheadon uses the analogy of school fences: we do not build fences because we think children are broken or disobedient; we build them because children run. In the same way, schools need behavior systems not because they expect failure but because they understand how humans develop. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory (Deci and Ryan), Steinberg's developmental psychology, and Lewin's person-environment model, the article makes the case that defiance at adolescence is not an anomaly to be eliminated but a predictable feature to be designed around. The most effective behavior systems, Wheadon concludes, assume students are still learning to make decisions and provide the clear, consistent structure within which that learning can happen safely — the fence that makes the running possible.
points: Boundary testing is not evidence that young people are broken — it is evidence that they are developing; the adolescent drive for autonomy is a core psychological need identified by Self-Determination Theory, not a behavioral pathology to be corrected.

Schools need behavior systems not because they expect children to fail but because they understand how humans develop: children forget, act impulsively, seek status, and test limits — all of which are developmental features, not defects.

The most effective behavior systems do not assume students will always make good choices; they assume students are still learning how to make them, and they provide the structure within which that learning can happen safely.

Behavior systems often become more important, not less, as students get older: the developmental drive for autonomy increases precisely at the point where academic demands, social complexity, and required decision-making also increase.

Effective schools treat defiance as a predictable feature of development to be designed around rather than an anomaly to be eliminated — the fence that makes the running possible without making the running dangerous.
quotes: We do not view running as a behavioural failure. We do not gather staff together to debate why children insist on sprinting across fields. We do not conclude that children are disrespectful because they occasionally break into a run. We recognise it as a predictable feature of childhood and design environments accordingly. In the same way, schools need rules because children test boundaries.

Boundary testing is not evidence that young people are broken. It is evidence that they are developing. The task for schools is not to eliminate defiance, but to design systems that make it safe, consistent, and educationally productive.

As children move into adolescence, they become increasingly motivated by autonomy. They want greater control over decisions, more independence, and a stronger sense of ownership over their lives. They begin to question rules and expectations they previously accepted without hesitation.

Developmental psychologists have long argued that establishing autonomy is a central task of adolescence. Research shows that increasing independence from parents and authority figures is a normal feature of adolescent development rather than a sign of dysfunction.

The most effective behaviour systems do not assume students will always make good choices. They assume students are still learning how to make them. This is why behaviour systems often become more important, not less important, as students get older.

As Kurt Lewin argued, behaviour is a function of both the person and their environment. Effective schools recognise that behaviour is shaped not only by individual choices but by the structures surrounding those choices.
